client: I lost my grandmother about a month ago, and ever since then, family gatherings have felt almost unbearable. Everyone else seems to be moving on and laughing and talking like normal, but I just sit there feeling this huge weight where she used to be. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try.
therapist:
It takes real courage to reach out even when part of you doubts it will help, and I'm really glad you did. The weight you're describing — that hollow, heavy space where she used to be — makes complete sense, especially when the world around you seems to keep spinning as if nothing has changed. 

Can you tell me a little more about what goes through your mind in those moments at family gatherings when you notice everyone else laughing and you're sitting with that weight?

client: At those gatherings, I just keep watching everyone and thinking, how are they doing this? Like, don't they remember she's gone, or did they just... move on without me? And then I start feeling guilty, like maybe something's wrong with me for not being able to laugh along with them.
therapist:
What you're experiencing - that sense of being stranded in grief while others seem to move forward - is such a painful and lonely place to be, and the guilt on top of it makes it even heavier to carry. I want to gently offer another way to look at it though: is it possible that others are grieving too, just expressing it differently, and that your deep sadness is actually a reflection of how much she meant to you rather than something being "wrong" with you? 

When that thought - "something is wrong with me" - shows up, what does it feel like it says about you as a person?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but it's hard not to feel like everyone else has just figured out how to keep going, and I'm still stuck. When that thought comes up, it feels like it's saying I'm weak, or that I loved her wrong somehow, like if I really had my life together I'd be able to handle this better. I know that probably sounds irrational, but it's such a loud voice that it drowns out the more reasonable stuff.
therapist:
That voice calling you "weak" is so loud and convincing, but I want to pause on something — the idea that grieving deeply means you "loved her wrong" is actually the opposite of the truth; this pain exists *because* the love was real and profound. It doesn't sound irrational at all that the louder, harsher voice drowns out the gentler one, because grief can make our inner critic incredibly powerful, but that doesn't make it accurate.

If a close friend came to you one month after losing someone they deeply loved and said "I think I'm weak for still struggling," what would you want them to know?

client: I'd probably tell them they're being too hard on themselves, that losing someone you love is one of the hardest things a person can go through. But when I try to turn that around and say it to myself, it just... doesn't land the same way. It feels like I'm making excuses for myself, like I'm letting myself off the hook for something I should be handling better by now.
therapist:
That gap you're noticing — where compassion flows so naturally toward a friend but feels like "making excuses" when you turn it toward yourself — is actually one of the most important things we could explore together, because it tells us something about the standard you're holding yourself to. The fact that you *can* access that compassion, even if it doesn't fully land yet, means it's there inside you; it just has to fight through a very harsh inner judge who seems to believe you need to earn the right to grieve. 

Where do you think that voice learned that grief is something you're supposed to "handle" rather than simply move through at your own pace?

client: I think that voice came from watching my dad growing up — he never really let himself fall apart over anything, and I always got the sense that emotions were something you pushed through, not something you sat with. When my grandmother died and I cried for weeks, he didn't say anything mean exactly, but there was this look, like I was being self-indulgent. I guess I internalized that grief has a kind of expiration date, and if you're still feeling it past that point, something is wrong with you.
therapist:
What you just shared is really significant — you didn't arrive at this harsh standard on your own, you learned it from someone you loved and looked up to, in a household where emotions were something to push through rather than feel. That look from your father carried a whole message that a younger version of you absorbed deeply, and it makes so much sense that his voice became your inner voice, even now when you're the one grieving him losing *his* mother. 

I'm wondering — now that you can see where that "expiration date" belief came from, does it feel like it belongs to you, or does it feel more like something that was handed to you that you've been carrying without ever choosing it?

client: That question kind of stopped me in my tracks, honestly. When you put it that way, it does feel more like something I inherited than something I actually chose to believe — like I picked up a rule that was never mine to begin with. But I don't know, it's been inside me for so long that I'm not sure I even know how to separate what's his voice from what's actually mine.
therapist:
That moment of recognition — realizing a belief was inherited rather than chosen — is genuinely meaningful, and it's okay that untangling it feels difficult after carrying it for so long. The fact that you can now *notice* the voice and question whether it belongs to you is actually the first and most important step, because you can't choose to set something down until you can see that you're holding it.

As you sit with that idea, I'm curious — is there any part of you, even a quiet one, that has a different sense of what *your* voice might say about how long grief should last or how it should look?

client: I think there's a quiet part of me that believes grief doesn't really have a deadline, that it's more like... it changes shape over time rather than disappearing. But honestly, that voice feels really small and uncertain compared to the louder one that keeps telling me I should be over it by now. It's hard to trust the quieter voice when I've spent so long believing the other one was just the truth.
therapist:
That quiet voice — "grief changes shape rather than disappearing" — is actually a beautifully wise and accurate way to understand loss, and I don't think it's small at all; I think it's been there all along, just waiting for some space to be heard. It makes complete sense that it feels uncertain compared to the louder one, because the louder voice has had decades of practice while this gentler one is just beginning to be listened to.

What do you think that quieter voice might need from you in order to feel a little safer to trust?

client: I think that quieter voice needs me to stop immediately dismissing it when the louder one shows up and drowns it out. But honestly, that feels almost impossible to do in the moment, because the louder voice is so fast and so convincing that by the time I even realize what happened, I'm already deep in the guilt and the grief feels buried again. I guess what I'm saying is, I don't know how to slow down enough to even catch it.
therapist:
What you're describing — the louder voice moving so fast that you're already caught in guilt before you even notice it happened — is incredibly common, and it doesn't mean you're failing at this; it just means we need to find a way to create even a small pause between the trigger and the spiral. One gentle experiment might be to practice noticing the voice *after the fact* at first, not in the moment — like a kind of quiet reflection later where you simply say "there it was again," without any pressure to have caught it in real time.

Does it feel like there might be a low-pressure moment in your day — maybe in the evening or before sleep — where you could begin to gently notice when that louder voice visited you, almost like an observer rather than someone who had to fight it?

client: I mean, maybe... but honestly, evenings are kind of the worst time for me. That's usually when I'm alone and already feeling the loneliness creeping in, so sitting with my thoughts then feels like it could just make everything spiral even more. I'm not sure I want to invite more reflection when I'm already in that vulnerable place.
therapist:
That's really important feedback, and I'm glad you pushed back on that — the last thing I want is to suggest something that drops you into a harder place when you're already feeling vulnerable and alone. You know yourself well enough to recognize that evenings aren't the right container for this right now, and that self-awareness is actually worth trusting.

Is there a different time of day when you tend to feel even slightly more grounded or settled — maybe a morning moment, or a quiet pause during the day — where that kind of gentle noticing might feel a little safer to try?

client: Mornings are actually a little better, I think — at least before the day starts piling up and I start second-guessing everything I have to do. But even then, it's not like I wake up feeling great; there's usually this low-level dread sitting in my chest before I've even checked my phone. I'm not sure if that's really "grounded" enough to try something new, or if I'm just setting myself up to feel worse when it doesn't work.
therapist:
That low-level dread in the morning is real and worth acknowledging, and I don't want to minimize it — but I also notice that you described mornings as "a little better," which tells me there's something there, even if it's not perfect peace. What if "grounded enough" doesn't have to mean feeling good, but just means having a small sliver of space before the day rushes in — and what if we made the experiment so small that "not working" wasn't really possible, like simply placing a hand on your chest and acknowledging "this is hard right now" for just a few seconds?

What does it bring up for you to imagine being that gentle with yourself, even just for a brief moment in the morning?
